slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code defines a Vue.js component that calculates and stores polygon coordinates for a squircle shape using trigonometric functions, exposing these as CSS custom properties for styling, resulting in dynamic generation of smooth rounded shapes with no external communication.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code defines a Vue.js component that calculates polygon coordinates for a squircle shape and exposes these as CSS custom properties for styling. It uses standard JavaScript math functions and Vue lifecycle hooks without any obfuscation, network communication, environment variable checks, or destructive DOM manipulation. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks any suspicious or malicious behavior such as environment-based sabotage, external script loading from suspicious domains, or emptying the DOM. The code is purely for UI rendering purposes and does not perform any unauthorized or harmful actions.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.

package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects all repository versions where the workflow or JS patch is committed)
package_info.why_malicious: The campaign leverages stolen GitHub personal access tokens to inject malicious GitHub Actions workflows and append obfuscated JavaScript code to hundreds of repositories. The injected workflow exfiltrates all repository secrets and variables to an attacker-controlled server on every push event, while the patched JavaScript files load a remote payload that intercepts user credentials from password forms and exfiltrates them. The attacker disguises these commits as Dependabot updates to evade detection, resulting in a large-scale supply chain attack targeting both CI/CD secrets and end-user credentials.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains developer's GitHub personal access token (likely via a malicious package or environment compromise).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can authenticate as the victim on GitHub.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses stolen token to push fake Dependabot commits to victim's repositories, adding a malicious GitHub Actions workflow and appending obfuscated code to JavaScript files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the repository and will execute on CI/CD and in browsers.

attack_chain.action: On every push, the malicious GitHub Action exfiltrates repository secrets and variables to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive repository secrets.

attack_chain.action: When end-users load the compromised JavaScript files in their browsers, the appended code loads a remote script that intercepts password forms and exfiltrates credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives user credentials submitted via web forms.

behavioral_signatures: Creation or modification of GitHub Actions workflow files that POST secrets or variables to external, non-corporate domains
Mass modification of *.js files with appended obfuscated code that injects a script tag loading a remote payload
Commits with fake Dependabot or bot-like messages introducing suspicious workflow or JavaScript changes
Browser JavaScript code that hooks password forms and sends serialized credentials to unknown endpoints
file_indicators: .github/workflows/hook.yml
Any *.js file with appended obfuscated code that injects a script tag referencing send.wagateway.pro/client.js
Script tags in HTML referencing send.wagateway.pro/client.js
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan repository JavaScript files for appended obfuscated code that injects remote scripts, especially those referencing send.wagateway.pro. Flag commits with bot-like or fake Dependabot messages that introduce such changes. In browser environments, detect scripts that hook password forms and send data to non-corporate endpoints. Block or alert on network traffic to known malicious domains such as send.wagateway.pro. Correlate these indicators to identify supply chain compromise.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (template rendering), the code loads a stylesheet from an external domain (fonts.googleapis.com), causing the application to make a network request to fetch remote CSS, which could be replaced with malicious content.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading CSS from an external, uncontrolled domain introduces the risk that the remote resource could be modified to deliver malicious payloads, such as CSS-based exfiltration or further script injection if the server is compromised.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard application templates should only reference trusted, vetted, or self-hosted assets. Loading resources from external domains not under organizational control increases the risk of supply chain attacks and content injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use includes loading fonts or stylesheets from well-known, trusted CDNs (e.g., Google Fonts), but only when the CDN is explicitly trusted and the risk is assessed.
key_indicators: External stylesheet loaded at runtime
Reference to fonts.googleapis.com in HTML <link> tag
Network request to a domain not under organizational control
Potential for remote content replacement or injection

attack_chain.action: Application template loads an external stylesheet from fonts.googleapis.com at runtime.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for an attacker to replace or inject malicious CSS or further payloads via the external resource, increasing the risk of content injection or data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: Loading external stylesheets or scripts from remote domains in application templates
Presence of <link> or <script> tags referencing non-whitelisted domains in HTML files
file_indicators: templates/*.html files containing <link> tags with href attributes pointing to external domains (e.g., fonts.googleapis.com)
Configuration or template files referencing domains not on an approved whitelist
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to fonts.googleapis.com or other non-whitelisted domains during template rendering
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan HTML template files for <link> or <script> tags referencing external domains not on an approved whitelist. Monitor runtime network activity for outbound requests to non-whitelisted domains such as fonts.googleapis.com. Flag any executable or style content loaded from remote sources that are not explicitly approved by security policy.
